title: Saved from what, and how, “in childbearing” (1 Timothy 2:15)?
summary: 1 Timothy 2:15 says “she shall be saved in childbearing, if they continue in faith and charity and holiness with sobriety”. The verse does not say what the saving is from or to, how childbearing stands to being saved, who “she” is after the woman of 2:14, or who “they” are.
text: KJV 1 Timothy 2:15: “she shall be saved in childbearing, if they continue in faith and charity and holiness with sobriety”. Greek New Testament (Tischendorf, eighth edition) 1 Timothy 2:15: σωθήσεται δὲ διὰ τῆς τεκνογονίας, ἐὰν μείνωσιν ἐν πίστει καὶ ἀγάπῃ καὶ ἁγιασμῷ μετὰ σωφροσύνης [she will be saved through the childbearing, if they remain in faith and love and holiness with soberness]; the Textus Receptus text served prints the same words. KJV 1 Timothy 2:14: “the woman being deceived was in the transgression”. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/TISCH/54/2/ and https://bolls.life/get-text/TR/54/2/.
reasoning: The verse states a promise (“she shall be saved”) and a condition (“if they continue”). The verb is singular and the condition plural, and the verse does not say whether “she” is the woman of 2:14, women in general, or one woman, or whether “they” are the woman and others, or women in general. The Greek printed is διὰ τῆς τεκνογονίας, with a preposition and the article before “childbearing”, where the KJV prints “in” and no article. The verse does not say what the saving is from or how childbearing bears on it. Possible readings: preserved through the experience of childbirth; saved through the bearing of a particular child; saved while keeping to the role of bearing children; none of these is stated in the verses quoted and the record does not choose among them.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. The question is limited to 1 Timothy 2:14–15. A word search of the packaged KJV finds “childbearing” only at 1 Timothy 2:15. The record does not say which reading is right and does not claim that no other passage of the Bible says more. The Greek quoted is Tischendorf’s eighth edition as served by bolls.life, checked against the Textus Receptus text served there. The Greek New Testament wording is Tischendorf’s eighth edition as served by bolls.life (TISCH), compared with the Textus Receptus text served there (TR); neither is a critical apparatus.

title: Whose repentance, and what did Esau seek “with tears” (Hebrews 12:17)?
summary: Hebrews 12:17 says Esau “was rejected: for he found no place of repentance, though he sought it carefully with tears”. The verse does not say in terms whether “it” is the blessing or repentance, nor whose repentance finds no place, his own or a change of mind in the one who gave the blessing.
text: KJV Hebrews 12:17: “he found no place of repentance, though he sought it carefully with tears”. Greek New Testament (Tischendorf, eighth edition) Hebrews 12:17: μετανοίας γὰρ τόπον οὐχ εὗρεν, καίπερ μετὰ δακρύων ἐκζητήσας αὐτήν [for he found no place of repentance, although seeking it out with tears]; the Textus Receptus text served prints the same words in this clause. KJV Hebrews 12:16: “Esau, who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright”. KJV Genesis 27:34: “Bless me, even me also, O my father”. KJV Genesis 27:38: “Esau lifted up his voice, and wept”. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/TISCH/58/12/ and https://bolls.life/get-text/TR/58/12/.
reasoning: The verse says he “found no place of repentance” and that he sought “it” with tears. The pronoun printed in the Greek after “seeking out” is αὐτήν, and the clause just before it names “the blessing” (12:17) and “repentance” (the same verse); the verse does not say which one the pronoun points to. “No place of repentance” does not say whose repentance is meant, whether Esau’s own turning or a change of mind in his father. The two Genesis verses quoted report that Esau asked for a blessing and wept, and neither uses the word “repent”. Possible readings: he sought the blessing with tears and could not move his father to change his mind; he sought a way to repent and found none; and others; the record does not choose among them.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. The question is limited to Hebrews 12:16–17 with Genesis 27:34 and 27:38 quoted for context. Only the two Genesis verses were checked for the word “repent”; the rest of Genesis 27 was not read for this record. The record does not say which reading is right. title: Who were Jannes and Jambres (2 Timothy 3:8)?
summary: 2 Timothy 3:8 says “Jannes and Jambres withstood Moses”. The verse names two men and says what they did, but does not say who they were. The three Exodus verses compared speak of “the wise men”, “the sorcerers” and “the magicians of Egypt” and name none of them.
text: KJV 2 Timothy 3:8: “Jannes and Jambres withstood Moses”. Greek New Testament (Tischendorf, eighth edition) 2 Timothy 3:8: Ἰάννης καὶ Ἰαμβρῆς ἀντέστησαν Μωϋσεῖ [Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses]; the Textus Receptus text served prints the same words. KJV Exodus 7:11: “the magicians of Egypt, they also did in like manner with their enchantments”. KJV Exodus 7:22: “the magicians of Egypt did so with their enchantments”. KJV Exodus 8:7: “the magicians did so with their enchantments”. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/TISCH/55/3/ and https://bolls.life/get-text/TR/55/3/.
reasoning: The verse treats the two names as known to the reader and gives no account of them. The Exodus verses compared report the magicians as a group and give no names. The verse does not say whether Jannes and Jambres were among those magicians, when they withstood Moses, or where the names come from. Possible readings: they were two of the magicians of Exodus 7–8; they are named in a source the verse does not cite; they stand for others who withstood Moses at another time; the record does not choose among them. A word search of the packaged KJV finds “Jannes” and “Jambres” only at 2 Timothy 3:8.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. The question is limited to 2 Timothy 3:8 and the three Exodus verses quoted. The record does not say which reading is right and does not claim that no other ancient text names them. A published record compares what the magicians could and could not do; it does not ask who they were.
